At the start of this chapter we compared the words used in sceptical and supportive statements about immigration,
using a simple proportion. Now that we know about weighted log odds, we can redo that comparison properly.

::: {.exercise}
Compare the words used in sceptical and supportive statements using weighted log odds.
Use the same sentences as in the opening example:
sentences about immigration (not integration) with a sceptical or supportive direction, from all English-language countries.
It's up to you to decide which cleaning steps make sense here.
The result should be a data frame with the weighted log odds for each word and direction,
shown in descending order of log odds.

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ['ex_compare_direction', 'ex_compare_direction_challenge']
library(tidyverse)
library(tidytext)
library(tidylo)
pimpo <- read_csv("data/pimpo.csv")
pimpo_en <- filter(pimpo, country != "Austria")
country_words <- tibble(word=c("ireland", "irish", "america", "american", "americans", "united", "states"))
party_words <- pimpo_en |>
  filter(country %in% c("United States", "Ireland")) |>
  select(party) |>
  unnest_tokens(input = party, output = word) |>
  distinct()
custom_stopwords <- bind_rows(country_words, party_words)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_compare_direction
pimpo_en
```

::: { .hint exercise="ex_compare_direction"}
::: { .callout-tip title="Hint:"}
The steps are the same as in the country comparison above, so have a look at that code.

- First select the right sentences, then split them into words.
- Do you want to remove the possessive `'s` or stop words, as discussed above?
- Then count how often each word is used in each direction.
- Make sure that every word has a count for *both* directions, even if it is zero.
- Compute the log odds: which column defines the two groups that you are comparing?
- Arrange by log odds (descending) to show the most typical words.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_compare_direction"}
::: { .callout-important icon=false title="🎓 Solution:"}

- Use `filter(topic == "immigration", direction != "neutral")` to select the sentences. As `pimpo_en` only contains English-language countries, there is no need to filter on country.
- Tokenize with `unnest_tokens`. We chose to remove the possessive `'s` with `str_remove`, but to keep the stop words, as words like *we* or *our* can say a lot about how parties frame immigration. Removing (or keeping) the `'s` or stop words would also be fine, as long as you can justify your choice.
- Use `count(direction, word)` to count each word per direction.
- Use `complete()` to add a zero count for words that are only used in one direction. If you skip this step, `bind_log_odds` doesn't know that these words were never used in the other direction, and their log odds will be wrong.
- `bind_log_odds(direction, word, n)` compares the two directions.
- `arrange` to see the most typical words.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_compare_direction
#| solution: true
pimpo_en |>
  filter(topic == "immigration", direction != "neutral") |>
  unnest_tokens(text, output=word) |>
  mutate(word = str_remove(word, "['’]s$")) |>
  count(direction, word) |>
  complete(direction, word, fill = list(n = 0)) |>
  bind_log_odds(direction, word, n) |>
  arrange(desc(log_odds_weighted))
```

Sceptical statements are characterized by *illegal*, *border(s)*, *enforcement*, *aliens*, *boats* and *enter*,
while supportive statements talk about *refugees*, *rights*, *visa*, *family* and *reform*.
This is quite similar to the opening example, but the log odds also pick up more frequent words that are only somewhat overused,
such as *illegal* (22 times in sceptical statements) or even *a* in supportive statements.
:::
:::

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_compare_direction
#| check: true

gradethis::grade_this({
  if (is.data.frame(.result)) {
    # Diagnose the steps in order, so a partial pipeline gets a hint for the next step
    gradethis::fail_if("topic" %in% names(.result) && any(.result$topic != "immigration"),
      "Start by filtering the data to keep only the sentences about immigration (not integration or other topics).")
    gradethis::fail_if("direction" %in% names(.result) && any(is.na(.result$direction) | .result$direction == "neutral"),
      "Your data still contains neutral statements -- filter them out so you only keep sceptical and supportive sentences.")
    gradethis::fail_if("text" %in% names(.result),
      "Good start! Now split the sentences into words with `unnest_tokens`.")
    gradethis::fail_if(!"word" %in% names(.result),
      "We can't find a `word` column -- did you split the sentences into words with `unnest_tokens(text, output=word)`?")
    gradethis::fail_if(!"n" %in% names(.result),
      "Now count how often each word is used in each direction.")
    gradethis::fail_if(!any(.result$n == 0),
      "None of your words has a count of zero yet. Make sure every word has a count for both directions, even if it is zero (see `complete()` in the country comparison). Without the zeros, the log odds for words used in only one direction will be wrong.")
    gradethis::fail_if(!"log_odds_weighted" %in% names(.result),
      "Now compute the log odds with `bind_log_odds`.")
    gradethis::fail_if(!"direction" %in% names(.result),
      "We can't find a `direction` column -- are you comparing the words per direction?")
    # Accept all four combinations of removing (or keeping) the 's and stop words
    reference <- function(remove_s, remove_stopwords) {
      words <- get("pimpo_en", envir = .envir_result) |>
        dplyr::filter(topic == "immigration", direction != "neutral") |>
        tidytext::unnest_tokens(text, output = word)
      if (remove_s) words <- dplyr::mutate(words, word = stringr::str_remove(word, "['’]s$"))
      if (remove_stopwords) words <- dplyr::anti_join(words, tidytext::stop_words, by = "word")
      words |>
        dplyr::count(direction, word) |>
        tidyr::complete(direction, word, fill = list(n = 0)) |>
        tidylo::bind_log_odds(direction, word, n)
    }
    matches <- function(ref) {
      joined <- dplyr::inner_join(.result, ref, by = c("direction", "word"))
      nrow(.result) == nrow(ref) && nrow(joined) == nrow(ref) &&
        isTRUE(all.equal(joined$log_odds_weighted.x, joined$log_odds_weighted.y))
    }
    correct <- matches(reference(TRUE, FALSE)) || matches(reference(FALSE, FALSE)) ||
      matches(reference(TRUE, TRUE)) || matches(reference(FALSE, TRUE))
    gradethis::fail_if(correct && is.unsorted(-.result$log_odds_weighted),
      "Almost there! Now sort the result in descending order of log odds, so the most typical words come first.")
    gradethis::pass_if(correct,
      "Well done! You found the log odds for each word and direction. Have a look at the solution to see which cleaning steps we chose.")
    gradethis::fail(
      "Your result is different from ours. Check your filter: we want only sentences about immigration (not integration) that are sceptical or supportive. If you used other cleaning steps than removing the `'s` or the standard `stop_words`, your result may well be fine -- compare it with the solution.")
  }

  {{< include exercises/_check.qmd >}}
})
```
:::

::: {.challenge title="Australia versus the US"}
- Which of the two comparisons (the proportions at the start of the chapter, or the log odds above) tells you more about how sceptical parties talk about immigration? Why?
- Can you change the code below to compare Australian and American manifestos? What do you notice about the top words? How can you fix this?

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_compare_direction_challenge
pimpo_en |>
  filter(topic %in% c("immigration", "integration"),
         country %in% c("United States", "Ireland")) |>
  unnest_tokens(text, output=word) |>
  mutate(word = str_remove(word, "['’]s$")) |>
  anti_join(custom_stopwords) |>
  count(country, word) |>
  complete(country, word, fill = list(n = 0)) |>
  bind_log_odds(country, word, n) |>
  arrange(desc(log_odds_weighted))
```
:::
